content: Fusidic acid is a bacteriostatic antibiotic that is commonly applied topically in the form of creams and eye drops. It can also be administered systemically as tablets or injections. Pharmacology Fusidic acid functions by disrupting bacterial protein synthesis. Specifically, it inhibits the translocation of elongation factor G (EF-G) from the ribosome, which is a critical step in bacterial protein production. This antibiotic is effective only against gram-positive bacteria, such as Staphylococcus species and Corynebacterium species. It does not kill bacteria but instead inhibits their replication, which is why it is classified as bacteriostatic. Fusidic acid is a true antibiotic, derived from the fungus Fusidium coccineum. It was developed by Leo Laboratories in Ballerup, Denmark, and introduced for clinical use in the 1960s. Additionally, it has been isolated from Mucor ramannianus and Isaria kogana. While it is not licensed for use in the United States, sodium fusidate (a form of fusidic acid) is approved for prescription use in the United Kingdom, Europe, Australia, and New Zealand. Uses Fusidic acid demonstrates in vitro activity against Staphylococcus aureus, most coagulase-negative staphylococci, Corynebacterium species, and most Clostridium species. However, it has no significant activity against streptococci, enterococci, or most gram-negative bacteria, with the exceptions of Neisseria, Moraxella, Legionella pneumophila, and Bacteroides fragilis. It is active both in vitro and clinically against Mycobacterium leprae but has only marginal activity against Mycobacterium tuberculosis. Its most important clinical application is its effectiveness against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), a potentially fatal hospital-acquired superbug. Many MRSA strains remain sensitive to fusidic acid. However, due to the low genetic barrier to resistance (a single point mutation can confer resistance), fusidic acid should never be used as monotherapy for MRSA infections. Instead, it should be combined with another antimicrobial agent, such as rifampicin. Dosing Fusidic acid should not be used alone to treat Staphylococcus aureus infections. The use of topical preparations, such as skin creams and eye ointments containing fusidic acid, is strongly associated with the development of resistance. This has led to concerns about the continued use of fusidic acid monotherapy in community settings. In Europe, topical preparations often combine fusidic acid with gentamicin to help prevent resistance development. The adult dosage of sodium fusidate depends on the indication. It can range from 250 mg twice daily to up to 750 mg three times daily. Skin conditions typically require the lower dose. Fusidic acid is available in tablet and suspension forms. An intravenous preparation is also available, but it is irritating to veins and can cause phlebitis. Most patients absorb the drug very well when taken orally, so intravenous administration is generally unnecessary, even for conditions like endocarditis (infection of the heart chambers). Pregnancy Caution There is insufficient evidence regarding the safety of fusidic acid during human pregnancy. The drug is known to cross the placental barrier. Side Effects Fusidic acid tablets and suspensions (e.g., Fucidin®) can occasionally cause liver disturbances, which may result in jaundice (yellowing of the skin and the whites of the eyes). This condition typically resolves after completing the course of treatment. Other related side effects include dark urine and lighter-than-usual stools, which also normalize after treatment ends. Patients should inform their doctors if they notice very dark urine, very pale stools, or yellowing of the skin or eyes. Resistance Fusidic acid is not licensed for use in the United States, and there are no Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute (CLSI) definitions for fusidic acid resistance. In other regions, susceptibility is defined as a minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of 0.5 mg/L or less, while resistance is defined as an MIC of 2 mg/L or more. For a 5 µg disc, susceptibility is indicated by a zone of inhibition of 22 mm or more, and resistance is indicated by a zone of 17 mm or less. Intermediate values are classified as intermediate resistance. Resistance mechanisms have been extensively studied in Staphylococcus aureus. The primary mechanism involves point mutations in the fusA gene, which encodes EF-G. These mutations alter EF-G, preventing fusidic acid from binding to it. Resistance is readily acquired when fusidic acid is used alone and often develops during treatment. However, resistance does not occur when fusidic acid is used in combination with other antibiotics. For this reason, fusidic acid should not be used as monotherapy for Staphylococcus aureus infections. Some bacteria also mediate resistance via the fusB gene, which is carried on a plasmid. The exact mechanism by which fusB confers resistance is unknown. Interactions Fusidic acid should not be used with quinolones, as they are antagonistic. When combined with rifampicin, the action of fusidic acid is either additive or synergistic. The drug is available as an ointment, cream, eye drops, or in tablet form.
